claim_text: "Quarantine" derives from the Venetian dialect "quaranta giorni" (forty days), the isolation period imposed on ships arriving from plague-affected ports during the 14th-century Black Death.

Exile (Latin "exilium") was formalized in Roman law as a punishment that removed a person from their community while leaving their legal existence intact elsewhere, distinct from execution or slavery.
"Parole" entered English from French "parole" (word, speech); a prisoner released "on parole" was released on their word or promise, not on unconditional release.

"Scapegoat" originates in William Tyndale's 1530 English translation of Leviticus 16, rendering a Hebrew ritual term as "(e)scape goat" — a goat symbolically burdened with a community's sins and released into the wilderness.

"Liminal" (Latin "limen", threshold) was popularized in anthropology by Victor Turner's extension of Arnold van Gennep's work on rites of passage, describing the ambiguous middle stage of a transition ritual.
"Pedagogue" derives from Greek "paidagogos" (child + leader); the role originally named not a teacher but the slave assigned to escort a boy to school and supervise his conduct along the way.
"Mortgage" entered English from Old French "mort gage," literally "dead pledge": the pledge dies either when the debt is fully repaid or when the debtor defaults and forfeits the property.

"Sabotage" derives from French "saboter" (to bungle, to walk noisily, from "sabot," a wooden shoe); the popular story that it originated from workers throwing shoes into machinery is a documented myth, not supported by the historical record — the original sense was deliberately poor workmanship, not destruction.

"Propaganda" entered English in reference to the "Congregatio de Propaganda Fide" ("Congregation for Propagating the Faith"), a committee of cardinals established by Pope Gregory XV in 1622 to oversee the Catholic Church's foreign missions.

"Orphan" derives from Greek "orphanos" (bereft, deprived), tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to change status or allegiance" — the same root produced Old Church Slavonic and Germanic words for servitude and inheritance.
"Hybrid" derives from Latin "hibrida," which named the offspring of a tame sow and a wild boar, before the word broadened around 1850 to mean the product of any two heterogeneous things.

"Nostalgia" was coined in 1688 by Swiss physician Johannes Hofer, combining Greek "nostos" (homecoming) and "algos" (pain), to name what he classified as a medical disease — severe homesickness — observed in Swiss populations living away from home.

"Taboo" entered English from Tongan "tapu" (sacred, forbidden) via Captain James Cook's 1777 account of his Pacific voyages; the English noun and verb forms were Cook's own innovations, not direct translations.
"Curfew" derives from Old French "cuevrefeu," literally "cover fire": a bell rung at a fixed evening hour in medieval towns, signaling households to bank their hearth fires and prevent conflagration.
